newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's spring sowing threatened by lack of funds.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's spring sowing threatened by lack of funds.

text.p: Agriculture, the one industry in Serbia that kept going through years of war and international sanctions, is on the verge of collapse, with no funds to update machinery or carry on production.

"Other industry sectors boast how they preserved their largely idle capacities during this period, but we kept up production and now our capacities are worn out," Miroslav Jovanovic, president of the Yugoslav chamber of commerce agriculture committee, told a meeting of the board on Thursday.
Producers said they feared they would be unable to meet the government's optimistic spring sowing plans unless funds were found soon and they were paid for last year's crops.
The government late last month presented a plan to clear an outstanding 800 million dinar debt to farmers, but farmers said it was too little, too late.
"It is not the same 800 million dinars in March as it was in October," Jovanovic said, referring to rising input costs and inflation.
The agriculture sector is widely seen as having prevented people from going hungry during the 3 1/2 years of sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro.

But the chamber's vice-president, Milutin Cirovic, said preserving social peace through agriculture alone was no longer acceptable. "Agriculture cannot be the pillar of social stability in the country any more."
Sanctions were lifted last October, easing access to imports of fuel, artificial fertiliser and herbicides, but lack of funds and credits remained a major problem.
Agricultural machinery was run down and there was no money to update it or buy spare parts.
The 1997 agricultural budget of 930 million dinars, down from one billion last year, had in real terms been halved by inflation.
"To put it simply, there is no more money for subsidies," Cirovic said.
A government source admitted financing remained a big problem and that only 135 million dinars had been secured while preparations for sowing alone would cost more than one billion.
"Primary agricultural production accounts for 7-8 percent of primary issue and more than 20 percent of GDP, and this gap could be narrowed," the same source said.

Forward contracts for selling agricultural produce, which have been issued by the Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency, will remain a means of securing funds, but other sources needed to be sought, such as a re-allocation of available National Bank of Yugoslavia credits.

Serbia's tractor industry, which has an annual capacity of some 45,000 tractors, last year produced barely 1,660, while imports of agricultural machinery are limited to what is not produced on the domestic market.
"In such a case, how can we speak of local production when there is practically none," a farm cooperative source said, urging more liberal import quotas.
Producers said the Serbian government's spring sowing plan was too ambitious and could fall short unless concrete measures were taken.
The government plans six percent agricultural output growth in 1997 against the previous year and a substantial increase in the sector's exports.
Yugoslavia has a total of 3.68 million hectares of arable land, of which around 2.37 million are to be sown this spring, the chamber of commerce said.
Some 1.4 million hectares will be sown with maize, 100,000 with sugar beet, 200,000 with sunflower, 80,000 with soy, 255,000 with vegetables and 190,000 with fodder crops.
Of the total, around 385,000 hectares are planned to be sown in the "socially-owned" sector and 1.98 million hectares on private farms. ($1=5.4 dinars)
--Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
